newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian police storm villa to arrest Mafia boss.
newsitem.headline: Italian police storm villa to arrest Mafia boss.

text.p: Scores of police stormed a Sicilian farmhouse on Friday to arrest Pietro Aglieri, one of Italy's most wanted Mafia godfathers who combined refined manners with a deadly reputation.

Palermo police chief Antonino Manganelli told a news conference Aglieri had been arrested with two mob hitmen at 10 a.m. (0800 GMT) after around 100 police officers used ladders to enter the grounds of the house east of Palermo.
Another 200 agents were involved in the operation, surrounding the premises and hiding in a nearby orange grove.
"This was a brilliant operation," Manganelli said. "It confirms the competence of the police, the presence of the state in Sicily and its ability to fight the Mafia.
"This signifies that the Mafia is not invincible. By arresting Aglieri, we have shown that Mafiosi are not heroes and that the people should not consider them to be unbeatable."
Aglieri, escorted by hooded police agents, was driven to police headquarters for questioning.
The arrest near the town of Bagheria came three days before his 38th birthday.
Police said Aglieri, bald and wearing jeans and a white T-shirt, had not uttered a word either at the time of his arrest or subsequently when he was taken to police headquarters.
"They behaved like real bosses," said Manganelli of Aglieri and hitmen Natale Gambino and Giuseppe La Mattina.
The operation was hailed as a severe blow to the organised crime gangs and was the most important Mafia arrest since that of Sicilian boss Giovanni Brusca last year.
Italy's most wanted man is fugitive boss Bernardo Provenzano but Aglieri ranked close behind him.
"This very important success is the concrete proof that the state is fully committed in the fight against the Mafia," said deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni.
Giancarlo Caselli, chief prosecutor of Palermo, said the arrest was a triumph for traditional police methods since it did not depend on the help of any Mafia turncoats.

"This operation was not carried out with the help of any 'pentiti' (turncoats) but merely followed classical investigating techniques. It shows that even without turncoats the state is able to fight the Mafia," he said.

Aglieri has been sentenced in absentia to life for murder, for killing octagenarian boss Benedetto Grado, although that has yet to become definitive in Italy's exhaustive appeals procedure, and to 12 years for drug trafficking.
La Mattina has also been sentenced to life while Gambino has been sentenced to 10 years in jail.
Some investigators believe that Aglieri may have taken control of Cosa Nostra after godfather Salvatore "The Beast" Riina was captured in 1993.
Police said they found an altar in the villa which might have been used for Mafia ceremonies.

Nicknamed "U Signurinu" (The Young Gentleman) in Sicilian dialect for his supposed elegance, Aglieri had been on the run since December 1989 and is considered by investigators to be a right-hand man of Provenzano and ally of Riina.
Educated to high school level in a Catholic seminary administered by the archbishopric of Monreale, Aglieri enjoyed a reputation as a Sicilian "dapper don".

But he stands accused of involvement in the car bomb killings of magistrates Paolo Borsellino and Giovanni Falcone in 1992 as well as of former European parliamentarian Salvo Lima who was gunned down in the same year.

Anna Maria Palma, the prosecutor at the trial of Borsellino's alleged killers in the Sicilian town of Caltanissetta, said Aglieri had pressed the button on the remote control of the device that killed the magistrate.
Brusca is accused of the same act against Falcone.
